## Blunt reality check (before we design anything)

This is where I earn my keep, so read this part twice.

**1. Your edge is latency, not intelligence.** A human reacts visually in ~200–250 ms. A vision bot can go screen-grab → decide → click in ~30–50 ms end-to-end. That gap *is* the entire project. Every design decision must protect it. Anything that adds 20 ms is a bug, not a feature.

**2. Your real enemy is prediction, not detection.** In this genre you don't click when the gap *is* aligned — you click when it *will be* aligned at the moment the knife lands. So we need angular velocity `ω`, gap angle `θ`, and throw travel time `t`; then fire at `t_fire = t_land − t`. Getting `ω` accurate is the hard part. Detection is the easy part.

**3. 60 Hz is your bottleneck, and it may kill the whole thing.** If your panel runs at 60 Hz, your information refreshes every 16.7 ms. At 2 rev/s that's ~12° of blind rotation per frame. Twelve degrees is enough to hit an existing knife instead of the gap. Two fixes: sub-frame interpolation (phase correlation between consecutive frames — works, but adds compute), or a high-refresh panel + a capture path that can actually keep up. **I need your refresh rate before I promise anything.**

**4. MSS alone probably won't be fast enough at full screen — and it doesn't need to be.** The trick is to grab only a small ROI (say 600×600 px around the log), not the whole desktop. That's how you get hundreds of FPS instead of dozens. Also worth knowing: MSS uses GDI BitBlt on Windows, which is fine and portable but not the fastest path. `dxcam` (Desktop Duplication API) is materially faster on Windows. If your rules say MSS, we start with MSS and I'll show you the measured ceiling; if it's too slow I'll tell you straight rather than pretend.

**5. Classic CV will fail on a spinning textured log.** Hough circles on a wooden block at speed = garbage. The correct approach is: lock the circle center **once** (it doesn't move), then track **only rotation** via a radial intensity profile or phase correlation on an annulus. Cheap, fast, sub-degree accurate. That's the design I'd argue for.

**6. "Click like a real user" is easier than you think — and you may not need hardware.** OS-level `SendInput` events arrive in the browser as `isTrusted = true`, indistinguishable from a physical mouse at the JavaScript layer. So an Arduino HID injector is **not** required for authenticity. It's only worth it if we need lower jitter or if Windows/browser input latency turns out to be the limiter. I'd start with software and measure, not build hardware on day one.

**7. Motion blur is real.** At high `ω` the log smears. Edge detection degrades exactly when you need it most. Correlation-based methods degrade gracefully; threshold-based methods fall off a cliff. This is not a detail — it determines the whole pipeline.

**8. One thing that could invalidate everything:** if the game has a charge/hold mechanic, or the throw isn't instantaneous, or the aim point isn't fixed, the model changes completely. I can't design against a game I haven't seen. That's the first thing I need.

## 4. Your benchmark file — this is the most important thing you gave me

Your own numbers, read properly:

| Test | FPS | Bytes/sec through GDI |
|---|---|---|
| 1920×1080 | **30.0** | 2,073,600 × 4 × 30 = **249 MB/s** |
| 1280×720 | **60.2** | 921,600 × 4 × 60 = **221 MB/s** |
| 640×720 | **60.0** | 1,843,200 × 60 = 110 MB/s |
| 400×400 | **60.2** | 640,000 × 60 = 38 MB/s |

Two separate hard ceilings, and **they're both real**:

1. **Full screen is bandwidth-capped at ~250 MB/s.** That's why 1080p gives you exactly half of 720p's rate. GDI `BitBlt` cannot carry a full 1080p desktop at 60 fps on your machine. **Never capture full screen. Ever.**
2. **Everything else is pinned at exactly ~60.2 fps regardless of size.** 400×400 and 1280×720 are *identical*. That is not a CPU limit — that's the **compositor refresh rate**. Your panel is **60 Hz**.

**Consequence, and I need you to sit with it:** the desktop image only *changes* 60 times a second. Capturing faster just copies the same frame twice. **Your information rate is 16.67 ms. Permanently. There is no code change that fixes this.** The game itself also renders at 60 fps, so the motion blur and frame quantization are baked into the game, not into our capture.

I want your confirmation on the Hz. Check *Settings → System → Display → Advanced display → refresh rate*. If it's not 60, my whole analysis changes. This is the single most important number in the project.

---

## 5. The math that decides whether this works

This is the part I need you to read twice, because it's the difference between a working bot and a party you're paying for.

Knife butt is 37 px. At r = 132: chord angle = 2·arcsin(18.5/132) = **16.1°**. So **any free gap under ~16° is a guaranteed death.** Minimum safe gap ≈ 3 full grid cells.

Timing window = (gap − 16°) ÷ ω:

| Gap | Rotation ω | Safe window | vs. one 16.7 ms frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| 45° | 360°/s (1 rev/s) | **81 ms** | 4.8 frames — comfortable |
| 30° | 360°/s | **39 ms** | 2.3 frames — fine |
| 30° | 720°/s (2 rev/s) | **19 ms** | **1.2 frames — one bad frame = death** |
| 20° | 720°/s | **11 ms** | hopeless on reaction |
| 20° | 1080°/s (3 rev/s) | **7 ms** | **physically impossible to react to** |

And the lead you must hold: the knife takes flight time **T** to cross from tip to log. You do *not* fire when the gap is at 180°. You fire when the gap is at **180° − ω·T**. If T = 120 ms and ω = 720°/s, that's a **86° lead**. Get ω wrong by 5% and you throw 4° off. Get T wrong by 10 ms and you're 7° off.

**The blunt conclusion:** at low speed this is trivial. At high speed, a 60 Hz panel gives you *less than one frame of margin*, and no amount of OpenCV cleverness creates information that doesn't exist. The only way through is **sub-frame prediction** — timestamp every frame, fit ω over the last N frames by least squares, extrapolate forward, then fire on a **high-resolution timer**, not on the next capture frame. Vision decides *whether*; a clock decides *when*.

**Strategic implication you're missing:** a score bet is not won by throwing fast. It's lost by dying. The bot's win condition is **zero misses**, which means it should throw only when the window is genuinely safe and tolerate slower pacing. Your friend will die at speed 3. The bot doesn't have to. **Consistency beats velocity.**

# Classical CV. Not an AI model. It's not close.

I'll give you the honest reason, then the one place AI actually earns its keep.

## Why AI is the wrong tool here

**1. This is a metrology problem, not a perception problem.**

AI answers *"what is this thing and roughly where is it?"* Your task is *"how many degrees did this thing rotate between frame 214 and frame 215, to within ±0.3°?"*

That's a measurement. You don't put a neural network on a spinning shaft to find its RPM — you use an optical encoder. This game **is** an optical encoder. The wood grain, the bark cracks, the concentric rings are the encoder's tick marks. They're already there, free, high-contrast. Throwing a CNN at that is like using a language model to add two numbers.

**2. Latency is your entire budget, and inference spends it.**

At 60 Hz you get **16.67 ms per frame**. Rough allocation:

| Stage | Cost |
|---|---|
| MSS grab, 400×400 ROI | 4–6 ms |
| Polar unwrap + correlation | **0.3–1.5 ms** |
| Decision + timer | < 1 ms |
| Input injection | 1–3 ms |
| **Total, classical** | **~7–11 ms — fits** |
| A CNN/segmentation add-on | **+5–30 ms — blows it** |

At 720°/s, **1 ms of processing = 0.72° of angular error.** A 10 ms inference wears 7.2° of error all by itself. Your safety window at that speed is ~19 ms total. You'd be spending half of it on an extra that gives you *nothing*.

**3. AI is less accurate at this, not more.**

A segmentation net gives you a mask. Mask boundaries carry ~1–2 px of noise. At r = 132 px, **1 px = 0.43°**. So a neural mask caps you at roughly ±1° *before* you even estimate rotation from it — and you still have to run a registration step on top.

Direct correlation of intensity profiles gets **0.1–0.5°** with parabolic peak interpolation. Ten times better, a hundred times cheaper.

**4. You have zero training data, and it would be wasted anyway.**

To train or fine-tune you'd need hundreds of labelled frames of *this specific game at these specific speeds*. That's days of work for a worse result. The correlation method needs **no training at all** — because rotation between two frames of the *same* textured object is a solved geometric problem, not a learned one.

**5. Determinism matters when you're betting a party on it.**

A correlation estimator either succeeds with a confidence score or explicitly fails. You can bound it, test it, and trust it. A neural net fails silently and differently each run. In a closed timing loop, "I don't know, so skip this frame" is a *feature* — and only classical CV gives it to you honestly.

---

## What I'll actually use

**Primary: radial-signature cross-correlation.** Unwrap a ring around the log's centre into angle × radius, average along radius → a 360–720 sample signature of the log's texture. Rotation shifts that signature. Cross-correlate consecutive frames → Δθ. Sub-bin accuracy from a parabolic fit on the correlation peak. Then ω = Δθ / Δt.

- **~0.2–0.5 ms per frame**
- **0.1–0.3° accuracy**
- Immune to brightness changes, the apples, the knives, and partial occlusion
- Works on this log specifically because it has strong radial structure

**Secondary: phase correlation** (Fourier-Mellin) on the same annulus as an independent check. If the two methods disagree by more than 0.5° on any frame, that frame gets flagged instead of trusted.

**Tertiary: sparse Lucas-Kanade optical flow** — only to determine rotation *direction* and catch reversals, which correlation handles poorly when the shift is near ±180°.

Three methods, one number, cross-validated. That's the standard. Not one method, blindly trusted.

---

## Where AI genuinely earns its place — offline

I'm not anti-AI, I'm anti-**AI-in-the-hot-loop**. There are three jobs where it wins:

1. **One-time ground truth.** Run a segmentation model (SAM / SegFormer) on a single clean reference frame to extract a precise log mask. From that: exact pivot, true radius, and the bevel offset I suspected earlier. Runs **once**, takes seconds, and permanently fixes your 949-vs-957 ambiguity.
2. **Score reading.** OCR on the score strip at 2 Hz. Not latency-critical, so a model is fine.
3. **Validation.** Run a dense optical-flow net offline over the video and compare its ω curve to my correlation curve. If they match, my numbers are proved. That's a *verification* tool, not a runtime one.

**Rule of thumb: AI for ground truth, classical for control.** Every high-speed vision system on earth is built that way.

---

## Now — what your 30 fps video does and doesn't cost you

**Doesn't hurt you:**
- **30 fps is plenty to measure ω.** No aliasing risk: ambiguity starts at 180° of rotation per frame, which at 30 fps means 5400°/s (15 rev/s). At a realistic 3 rev/s you'd get 36°/frame. Clean.
- **Screen recordings are easier than camera footage** — crisp frames, no motion blur, no rolling shutter, no lens distortion. Every frame is an exact pixel copy of what the GPU drew. That's a gift; phone footage would have been a nightmare.
- **Angles are scale-invariant.** The video is 1916×868 and your measurements are 1917×1077 — doesn't matter. Rotation in degrees survives any rescaling. Only the centre and radius need re-deriving per resolution. **Pixels don't transfer; angles do.**

**Does hurt you:**
- **30 fps is half of what the bot sees live.** Speed *tiers* will be measured accurately (they're constant regimes). But speed *changes* and reversals will be resolved to ±33 ms instead of ±17 ms. Acceptable for reporting min/avg/max — not acceptable for modelling the bot's real timing. I'll model the bot at 60 Hz and use the video only for ω.
- **Knife flight time will be rough.** A ~100 ms flight is 3 video frames. ±1 frame = ±33 ms of error. I'll average across many throws, but **flight time is better calibrated live**, by measurement, than guessed from this video.

**If you can re-record at 60 fps** (OBS, or Game Bar with the "high frame rate" capture), do it — it's a 2× improvement for free. But don't block on it. 47 seconds at 30 fps is enough to get your speed tiers.

---

## One terminology correction, because it will cause bugs later

You keep saying *"frequency of speed."* Those are two different quantities:

- **Speed / angular velocity `ω`** — degrees per second, rev/s, or RPM
- **Frequency** — revolutions per second (Hz). **1 rev/s = 360°/s = 60 RPM = 1 Hz**

When the game "changes speed," it changes **ω**. I'll report every tier in **°/s, rev/s, and RPM** so there's never an ambiguity about which one we mean. Small thing, but this is exactly the kind of loose language that produces a bot that throws at the wrong moment.

---

## So, to answer you flatly

**Python + OpenCV, classical, no AI in the runtime path.** AI only as an offline measuring stick and a validator. Anything else is slower, less accurate, untrainable on your data, and would eat the latency budget that is the entire reason this bot can beat a human.

**Say go** and I'll start: locate the log in the video, build the polar unwrap, extract the ω time series from all 1409 frames, cluster it into speed tiers, and report min / avg / max per tier in three units — with the secondary method as a cross-check and any disagreeing frames flagged rather than averaged away.

I'll also drop the one-time calibration (pivot, true radius, bevel offset) into `measurements/` at the same time, since it costs nothing extra.

```python
def signature(polar):
    # remove per-radius DC, then sum over radius
    p = polar.astype(np.float32)
    p = p - p.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    # normalize per radius by std to weight all radii equally
    s = p.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    s[s < 1e-3] = 1.0
    p = p / s
    sig = p.mean(axis=1)   # length N_THETA
    return sig
```

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""
find_speed.py
=============
Measure the rotational speed (angular velocity) of the Knife Rush target log
from a screen recording, with no AI model and no training data.

WHY THIS METHOD
---------------
The task is not "recognise the log". It is "how many degrees did the log rotate
between frame t and frame t+1". That is a metrology / signal-processing problem.

The wood grain, bark cracks and rim shading form a natural optical encoder.
Unwrap a ring of the log into (angle x radius), average across radius, and the
resulting 1-D signature is a periodic function of the log's rotation. Rotation
is then a pure circular shift between consecutive signatures, recovered by
cross-correlation to sub-bin precision.

  cost      : ~0.2 - 1.0 ms per frame on CPU
  accuracy  : ~0.1 - 0.3 degrees
  training  : none
  failure   : explicit -- a normalised confidence score per frame

A CNN would need training data nobody has, would be 5-30 ms per frame (blowing
the 16.7 ms budget of a 60 Hz loop), and would still cap out near +-1 degree
because a segmentation mask boundary carries 1-2 px of noise, and at r = 132 px
1 px == 0.43 degrees.
"""
```

```python
def circular_lag(a, b):
    n = a.size
    A = np.fft.rfft(a)
    B = np.fft.rfft(b)
    c = np.fft.irfft(A * np.conj(B), n=n)     # c[k] = sum_n a[n] b[n-k]
    k = int(np.argmax(c))
    # parabola through k-1, k, k+1
    y0 = c[(k - 1) % n]; y1 = c[k]; y2 = c[(k + 1) % n]
    denom = (y0 - 2.0 * y1 + y2)
    delta = 0.5 * (y0 - y2) / denom if abs(denom) > 1e-12 else 0.0
    delta = float(np.clip(delta, -0.5, 0.5))
    # b = roll(a, -k)  =>  lag L = -k
    lag = -(k + delta)
    lag = (lag + n / 2.0) % n - n / 2.0     # wrap to [-n/2, n/2)
    # confidence: normalised correlation at the peak
    denom_norm = math.sqrt(float(np.dot(a, a)) * float(np.dot(b, b))) + 1e-12
    conf = float(c[k]) / denom_norm
    ...
```

```python
    sharp = (c[k] - c[k2]) / (abs(c[k]) + 1e-12)
```

```python
def selftest(verbose=True):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    n = 720
    a = rng.normal(size=n)
    a = np.convolve(a, np.ones(5)/5, mode='same')  # smooth a bit
    for true_shift in (0, 1, 5, 37, -37, 100, -100):
        b = np.roll(a, true_shift)
        lag, conf, _ = circular_lag(a, b)
        assert abs(lag - true_shift) < 0.05, (true_shift, lag)
```

And I defined: c[k] = Σ a[n] b[n−k], peak at k means b[m] ≈ a[m+k]. With b = roll(a, s): b[m] = a[m−s]. So a[m+k] = a[m−s] → k = −s. So L = −k = s. ✓.

So `circular_lag(a, np.roll(a, s))` should return s. The assert checks that.

But hold on — I need to double check the direction of my signature indexing vs. actual rotation.

Signature s[θ] = intensity at angle θ. If the log rotates clockwise by Δθ, then the material that was at angle θ is now at angle θ+Δθ. So s_{t+1}(θ+Δθ) = s_t(θ), i.e., s_{t+1}(α) = s_t(α−Δθ), i.e., s_{t+1} = roll(s_t, +Δθ_bins). ✓

So lag = Δθ_bins, positive = clockwise. Good.

```python
def build_maps(cx, cy, r, n_theta, n_radius, inner_frac, outer_frac):
    th = np.arange(n_theta, dtype=np.float32) * (2*np.pi/n_theta)
    rr = np.linspace(inner_frac*r, outer_frac*r, n_radius, dtype=np.float32)
    cos_t = np.cos(th)[:, None]
    sin_t = np.sin(th)[:, None]
    mx = (cx + rr[None, :]*cos_t).astype(np.float32)
    my = (cy + rr[None, :]*sin_t).astype(np.float32)
    return mx, my
```

```
def fit_circle(pts):
    x = pts[:,0]; y = pts[:,1]
    A = np.c_[2*x, 2*y, np.ones(len(x))]
    b = x*x + y*y
    sol, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)
    cx, cy = sol[0], sol[1]
    r = math.sqrt(sol[2] + cx*cx + cy*cy)
    return cx, cy, r
```

```python
def detect_tiers(omega, fps, min_share=0.06):
    w = np.sort(np.abs(omega[valid]))
    # histogram
    lo, hi = np.percentile(w, [1, 99])
    if hi - lo < 1e-6: return []
    bins = np.arange(lo, hi + 1e-9, max(1.0, (hi-lo)/120))
    hist, edges = np.histogram(w, bins=bins)
    # smooth
    k = np.array([1,2,3,2,1], float); k/=k.sum()
    hs = np.convolve(hist.astype(float), k, mode='same')
    # local maxima
    peaks = []
    for i in range(1, len(hs)-1):
        if hs[i] >= hs[i-1] and hs[i] > hs[i+1]:
            peaks.append(i)
    # keep peaks with enough mass
    total = hist.sum()
    peaks = [p for p in peaks if hist[max(0,p-2):p+3].sum() >= min_share*total]
    ...
```

Unwraps an annulus of the log into a (angle x radius) polar image.\n     The inner radius is deliberately pulled in, to exclude the \"x1.01\"\n     multiplier text in the middle of the log -- that text does NOT rotate\n     with the log, and including it would bias every estimate toward zero.\n  3. Averages across radius to get a 1-D signature s(theta) -- a periodic\n     function of the log's rotation.\n  4. Recovers rotation as a circular shift between consecutive signatures,\n     by FFT cross-correlation, with parabolic sub-bin interpolation.\n  5. Cross-checks every frame with a second, independent-ish estimator that\n     correlates each radius ring separately instead of averaging first.\n  6. Converts to degrees/second, revolutions/second and RPM, then finds the\n     distinct speed tiers the game uses.\n\n  cost      ~0.3 - 1.5 ms per frame on CPU\n  accuracy  ~0.05 - 0.3 degrees per frame\n  failure   explicit: every frame carries a confidence score, and frames below\n            the threshold are dropped instead of silently averaged in.\n\n\nWHY NOT A NEURAL NETWORK\n------------------------\n  * A segmentation mask boundary carries 1-2 px of noise. At r = 132 px,\n    1 px = 0.43 deg. So a CNN caps out near +-1 deg BEFORE you even estimate\n    rotation from its mask. Cross-correlation gets 0.1-0.3 deg.\n  * Inference costs 5-30 ms. The whole 60 Hz budget is 16.7 ms.\n  * No training data exists for this specific game.\n  * A CNN fails opaquely; this fails with a number you can threshold.\n\nDeep learning is the right tool for a different job: producing a one-time\nground-truth mask of the log, offline. That is a separate script.\n\n\nUSAGE\n-----\n  python find_speed.py --video gameplay1.mp4\n  python find_speed.py --video gameplay1.mp4 --limit 200     # quick test\n  python find_speed.py --video gameplay1.mp4 --no-plot       # skip matplotlib\n  python find_speed.py --probe                               # metadata only\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nimport argparse\nimport csv\nimport json\nimport math\nimport os\nimport sys\nimport time\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing import Optional, Tuple\n\nimport cv2\nimport numpy as np\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n# Configuration\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n\n@dataclass\nclass Cfg:\n    video: str\n    outdir: str = \"measurements\"\n    n_theta: int = 1440          # angular bins -> 0.25 deg per bin\n    n_radius: int = 32           # radial rings sampled between inner/outer\n    inner_frac: float = 0.55     # inner radius as a fraction of the wood radius\n    outer_frac: float = 0.92     # outer radius as a fraction of the wood radius\n    min_conf: float = 0.25       # normalised correlation below this = reject\n    min_sharp: float = 0.05      # peak sharpness below this = ambiguous\n    max_deg_per_frame: float = 175.0   # physically impossible above this\n    detect_samples: int = 24     # frames used to lock the log's centre/radius\n    limit: Optional[int] = None  # process only the first N frames\n    probe: bool = False\n    plot: bool = True\n    verbose: bool = True\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n# Core estimator\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n\ndef circular_lag(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:\n    \"\"\"Estimate the circular shift L such that b ~= np.roll(a, L).\n\n    Returns (lag_in_bins, confidence, sharpness).\n\n    Derivation of the sign, so nobody has to guess:\n        c[k] = IDFT( FFT(a) * conj(FFT(b)) )[k] = sum_n a[n] * b[n-k]\n    A peak at index k therefore means a[n] ~= b[n-k], i.e. b[m] ~= a[m+k],\n    i.e. b = roll(a, -k). So L = -k. The unit test below enforces this.\n    \"\"\"\n    n = a.size\n    A = np.fft.rfft(a)\n    B = np.fft.rfft(b)\n    c = np.fft.irfft(A * np.conj(B), n=n)\n\n    k = int(np.argmax(c))\n\n    # Sub-bin refinement: parabola through the peak and its two neighbours.\n    y0 = c[(k - 1) % n]\n    y1 = c[k]\n    y2 = c[(k + 1) % n]\n    denom = y0 - 2.0 * y1 + y2\n    delta = 0.5 * (y0 - y2) / denom if abs(denom) > 1e-12 else 0.0\n    delta = float(np.clip(delta, -0.5, 0.5))\n\n    lag = -(k + delta)\n    lag = (lag + n / 2.0) % n - n / 2.0        # wrap into [-n/2, +n/2)\n\n    # Confidence: both inputs are unit-norm, so the peak value is the\n    # normalised correlation coefficient, bounded by [-1, 1].\n    conf = float(c[k])\n\n    # Sharpness: how much the best peak beats the best *distant* peak.\n    # A low value means the estimate is ambiguous (e.g. near 180 deg, or a\n    # frame where the log is not on screen at all).\n    mask = np.ones(n, dtype=bool)\n    for d in range(-5, 6):\n        mask[(k + d) % n] = False\n    k2 = int(np.argmax(np.where(mask, c, -np.inf)))\n    sharp = (c[k] - c[k2]) / (abs(c[k]) + 1e-12)\n\n    return float(lag), conf, float(sharp)\n\n\ndef normalise(v: np.ndarray) -> Optional[np.ndarray]:\n    \"\"\"Zero-mean, unit-norm. Returns None if the signal is flat (no texture).\"\"\"\n    v = v.astype(np.float64)\n    v = v - v.mean()\n    nrm = float(np.linalg.norm(v))\n    if nrm < 1e-6:\n        return None\n    return v / nrm\n\n\ndef signature_from_polar(polar: np.ndarray) -> Optional[np.ndarray]:\n    \"\"\"Collapse (angle x radius) -> 1-D angular signature.\n\n    Each radius ring is DC-removed and equalised before averaging, so a bright\n    bark ring does not drown out a faint inner ring, and slow radial brightness\n    gradients do not masquerade as angular structure.\n    \"\"\"\n    p = polar.astype(np.float64)\n    p = p - p.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)          # per-ring DC removal\n    sd = p.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)\n    sd = np.where(sd < 1e-2, 1e-2, sd)             # floor: don't amplify noise\n    p = p / sd\n    return normalise(p.mean(axis=1))\n\n\ndef per_ring_lag(prev: np.ndarray, cur: np.ndarray) -> Optional[float]:\n    \"\"\"Second estimator: correlate each radius ring separately, then take a\n    confidence-weighted median. Independent of the radial averaging in\n    signature_from_polar(), so the two disagreeing is a useful warning.\"\"\"\n    lags, weights = [], []\n    for j in range(prev.shape[1]):\n        a = normalise(prev[:, j])\n        b = normalise(cur[:, j])\n        if a is None or b is None:\n            continue\n        lag, conf, sharp = circular_lag(a, b)\n        if conf > 0.15:\n            lags.append(lag)\n            weights.append(max(conf, 0.0) * max(sharp, 0.01))\n    if len(lags) < 4:\n        return None\n    lags = np.asarray(lags)\n    weights = np.asarray(weights)\n    order = np.argsort(lags)\n    cw = np.cumsum(weights[order])\n    return float(lags[order][np.searchsorted(cw, 0.5 * cw[-1])])\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n# Target detection\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n\ndef _fit_circle(pts: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:\n    \"\"\"Algebraic (Kasa) least-squares circle fit.\"\"\"\n    x, y = pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1]\n    A = np.column_stack([2.0 * x, 2.0 * y, np.ones_like(x)])\n    b = x * x + y * y\n    sol, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)\n    cx, cy, c = sol[0], sol[1], sol[2]\n    r = math.sqrt(max(c + cx * cx + cy * cy, 1e-6))\n    return float(cx), float(cy), float(r)\n\n\ndef detect_target(frame: np.ndarray) -> Optional[Tuple[float, float, float]]:\n    \"\"\"Find the log: (cx, cy, radius) in frame pixels, or None.\n\n    Strategy: the log is the dominant warm-coloured blob. Its centroid is a\n    good first estimate; a radial scan outward from that centroid then gives a\n    boundary that is *robust* -- the median is taken, so the handful of rays\n    that pass through a protruding knife are discarded rather than inflating\n    the radius.\n    \"\"\"\n    h, w = frame.shape[:2]\n    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)\n\n    # Wood / orange-brown. Background is sky-blue and forest-green, so this\n    # isolates the log cleanly.\n    mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, (5, 80, 80), (34, 255, 255))\n\n    k = max(3, (int(round(min(h, w) * 0.015)) | 1))\n    mask = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE,\n                            cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (k, k)))\n    mask = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN,\n                            cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (5, 5)))\n\n    n_lab, labels, stats, cents = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(mask, 8)\n    if n_lab <= 1:\n        return None\n\n    areas = stats[1:, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA]\n    idx = 1 + int(np.argmax(areas))\n    box_w = stats[idx, cv2.CC_STAT_WIDTH]\n    box_h = stats[idx, cv2.CC_STAT_HEIGHT]\n    if box_w <= 0 or box_h <= 0:\n        return None\n    aspect = box_w / float(box_h)\n    if not (0.60 <= aspect <= 1.65):      # the log is round; reject slivers\n        return None\n    if areas[idx - 1] < 0.0015 * h * w:   # too small to be the log\n        return None\n\n    cx, cy = float(cents[idx][0]), float(cents[idx][1])\n    comp = (labels == idx)\n\n    # Radial scan: for each of 720 directions, the furthest radius still on the\n    # blob. The median of those distances is the real radius.\n    n_rays = 720\n    angs = np.arange(n_rays, dtype=np.float64) * (2.0 * math.pi / n_rays)\n    r_max = int(min(h, w) * 0.45)\n    boundary = []\n    for a in angs:\n        ca, sa = math.cos(a), math.sin(a)\n        hit = -1.0\n        for rr in range(4, r_max):\n            xx = int(cx + rr * ca)\n            yy = int(cy + rr * sa)\n            if 0 <= yy < h and 0 <= xx < w and comp[yy, xx]:\n                hit = float(rr)\n        if hit > 0:\n            boundary.append((cx + hit * ca, cy + hit * sa))\n\n    if len(boundary) < 180:\n        return None\n\n    pts = np.asarray(boundary, dtype=np.float64)\n    d = np.linalg.norm(pts - np.array([cx, cy]), axis=1)\n    r_med = float(np.median(d))\n\n    # Drop the spikes: rays that hit a protruding knife land far outside the\n    # median. Keep only points near the median radius.\n    keep = (d > r_med * 0.75) & (d < r_med * 1.12)\n    if keep.sum() < 90:\n        return None\n\n    fx, fy, fr = _fit_circle(pts[keep])\n    # Sanity: the refined centre must not wander far from the centroid.\n    if math.hypot(fx - cx, fy - cy) > 0.15 * r_med:\n        return cx, cy, r_med\n    return fx, fy, fr\n\n\ndef estimate_target(cap, cfg: Cfg) -> Tuple[float, float, float, dict]:\n    \"\"\"Lock the log's centre and radius using several frames, then take the\n    median. One frame is not enough: knives are stuck in it, and the log is\n    sometimes mid-throw.\"\"\"\n    total = int(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_COUNT)) or 0\n    step = max(1, total // max(1, cfg.detect_samples)) if total else 20\n\n    found = []\n    i = 0\n    while True:\n        ok, frame = cap.read()\n        if not ok:\n            break\n        if i % step == 0:\n            got = detect_target(frame)\n            if got is not None:\n                found.append(got)\n        i += 1\n        if total and i >= total:\n            break\n\n    cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_POS_FRAMES, 0)\n\n    if not found:\n        raise RuntimeError(\n            \"Could not find the log in any sampled frame. The hue range in \"\n            \"detect_target() probably needs tuning for this recording.\"\n        )\n\n    arr = np.asarray(found, dtype=np.float64)\n    cx, cy, r = (float(np.median(arr[:, 0])),\n                 float(np.median(arr[:, 1])),\n                 float(np.median(arr[:, 2])))\n\n    info = {\n        \"samples\": len(found),\n        \"cx_spread_px\": float(arr[:, 0].ptp()),\n        \"cy_spread_px\": float(arr[:, 1].ptp()),\n        \"r_spread_px\": float(arr[:, 2].ptp()),\n    }\n    return cx, cy, r, info\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n# Speed-tier analysis\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n\ndef _smooth(x: np.ndarray, k: int) -> np.ndarray:\n    if k < 3 or x.size < k:\n        return x.copy()\n    ker = np.ones(k, dtype=np.float64) / k\n    return np.convolve(x, ker, mode=\"same\")\n\n\ndef detect_tiers(speed: np.ndarray, min_share: float = 0.05) -> list:\n    \"\"\"Find the distinct speed plateaus the game uses.\n\n    A histogram of |omega| is built and smoothed; peaks carrying at least\n    `min_share` of the total occupancy are treated as tier centres. This is\n    deliberately simple and explainable -- if the game ramps continuously\n    instead of stepping, the 'coverage' figure below will come out low and\n    that is the honest answer.\n    \"\"\"\n    s = np.abs(speed)\n    if s.size < 30:\n        return []\n\n    lo, hi = np.percentile(s, [1, 99])\n    if hi - lo < 1e-6:\n        return []\n    bin_w = max(1.0, (hi - lo) / 120.0)\n    edges = np.arange(lo, hi + bin_w, bin_w)\n    hist, _ = np.histogram(s, bins=edges)\n    if hist.sum() == 0:\n        return []\n\n    hist = _smooth(hist.astype(np.float64), 5)\n    total = float(hist.sum())\n\n    peaks = []\n    for i in range(1, hist.size - 1):\n        if hist[i] >= hist[i - 1] and hist[i] > hist[i + 1]:\n            mass = hist[max(0, i - 2): i + 3].sum()\n            if mass >= min_share * total:\n                peaks.append(i)\n\n    if not peaks:\n        return []\n\n    # Merge peaks closer than 3 bins (they are the same plateau).\n    merged = [peaks[0]]\n    for p in peaks[1:]:\n        if p - merged[-1] > 3:\n            merged.append(p)\n\n    centres = np.array([0.5 * (edges[p] + edges[p + 1]) for p in merged])\n\n    # Assign every sample to its nearest tier centre.\n    idx = np.argmin(np.abs(s[:, None] - centres[None, :]), axis=1)\n    tiers = []\n    for i, c in enumerate(centres):\n        m = idx == i\n        if m.sum() < 10:\n            continue\n        vals = s[m]\n        tiers.append({\n            \"centre_deg_s\": float(c),\n            \"count\": int(m.sum()),\n            \"mean_deg_s\": float(vals.mean()),\n            \"min_deg_s\": float(vals.min()),\n            \"max_deg_s\": float(vals.max()),\n            \"std_deg_s\": float(vals.std()),\n            \"share\": float(m.sum() / s.size),\n        })\n    tiers.sort(key=lambda t: t[\"centre_deg_s\"])\n\n    # How much of the data actually sits on a plateau? A high number means\n    # discrete speed tiers are real; a low one means continuous acceleration.\n    near = np.min(np.abs(s[:, None] - centres[None, :]), axis=1)\n    coverage = float((near <= max(0.08 * float(np.median(centres)), 5.0)).mean())\n    for t in tiers:\n        t[\"coverage\"] = coverage\n    return tiers\n\n\ndef find_reversals(speed: np.ndarray, fps: float, thresh: float = 15.0):\n    \"\"\"Times at which the rotation direction flips. Knife Rush-style games\n    usually reverse the log at certain levels; the bot must know about it.\"\"\"\n    sign = np.sign(np.where(np.abs(speed) < thresh, 0, speed))\n    sign = sign[sign != 0]\n    if sign.size < 2:\n        return []\n    flips = np.where(sign[1:] != sign[:-1])[0]\n    return [(int(i), float(i / fps)) for i in flips]\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n# Self-test: kills the sign / off-by-one class of bug before it can lie to you\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n\ndef selftest() -> None:\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(12345)\n    n = 720\n    a = rng.normal(size=n)\n    a = np.convolve(a, np.ones(7) / 7.0, mode=\"same\")\n    a = normalise(a)\n    for true_shift in (0, 1, 5, 37, -37, 100, -100, 200):\n        b = np.roll(a, true_shift)\n        lag, conf, sharp = circular_lag(a, b)\n        if abs(lag - true_shift) > 0.05:\n            raise AssertionError(\n                f\"circular_lag sign/scale bug: expected {true_shift}, got {lag}\"\n            )\n        if conf < 0.99:\n            raise AssertionError(f\"confidence broken: {conf}\")\n    print(\"[selftest] circular_lag sign convention + sub-bin accuracy : PASS\")\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n# Main\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #\n\ndef main() -> int:\n    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=\"Measure log rotation speed from video.\")\n    ap.add_argument(\"--video\", default=\"gameplay1.mp4\")\n    ap.add_argument(\"--outdir\", default=\"measurements\")\n    ap.add_argument(\"--limit\", type=int, default=None, help=\"only first N frames\")\n    ap.add_argument(\"--no-plot\", action=\"store_true\")\n    ap.add_argument(\"--probe\", action=\"store_true\", help=\"metadata only, no analysis\")\n    ap.add_argument(\"--min-conf\", type=float, default=0.25)\n    args = ap.parse_args()\n\n    cfg = Cfg(video=args.video, outdir=args.outdir, limit=args.limit,\n              probe=args.probe, plot=not args.no_plot, min_conf=args.min_conf)\n\n    if not os.path.exists(cfg.video):\n        print(f\"ERROR: video not found: {cfg.video}\", file=sys.stderr)\n        return 2\n\n    cap = cv2.VideoCapture(cfg.video)\n    if not cap.isOpened():\n        print(f\"ERROR: OpenCV could not open {cfg.video}\", file=sys.stderr)\n        return 2\n\n    fps = float(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS)) or 30.0\n    total = int(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_COUNT))\n    width = int(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH))\n    height = int(cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT))\n    n_proc = min(total, cfg.limit) if cfg.limit else total\n\n    print(\"=\" * 74)\n    print(\"KNIFE RUSH - TARGET ROTATION SPEED MEASUREMENT\")\n    print(\"=\" * 74)\n    print(f\"video        : {cfg.video}\")\n    print(f\"resolution   : {width} x {height}\")\n    print(f\"frame rate   : {fps:.3f} fps  (dt = {1000.0 / fps:.3f} ms)\")\n    print(f\"frames       : {total}  ({total / fps:.2f} s)\")\n    if cfg.limit:\n        print(f\"limit        : processing first {n_proc} frames only\")\n    print()\n\n    if cfg.probe:\n        cap.release()\n        return 0\n\n    selftest()\n    print()\n\n    # ---- 1. lock the target ------------------------------------------------\n    t0 = time.perf_counter()\n    cx, cy, r_wood, det_info = estimate_target(cap, cfg)\n    print(f\"[target] centre = ({cx:.2f}, {cy:.2f})   wood radius = {r_wood:.2f} px\")\n    print(f\"[target] from {det_info['samples']} frames   \"\n          f\"spread: x {det_info['cx_spread_px']:.1f} px, \"\n          f\"y {det_info['cy_spread_px']:.1f} px, \"\n          f\"r {det_info['r_spread_px']:.1f} px\")\n    if det_info[\"cx_spread_px\"] > 8 or det_info[\"cy_spread_px\"] > 8:\n        print(\"[target] WARNING: centre drifts across the clip. If the window was \"\n              \"resized mid-recording, split the video and re-run per segment.\")\n    print(f\"[target] detection took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s\")\n    print()\n\n    r_in = r_wood * cfg.inner_frac\n    r_out = r_wood * cfg.outer_frac\n    print(f\"[annulus] r_in = {r_in:.1f} px ({cfg.inner_frac:.2f} R), \"\n          f\"r_out = {r_out:.1f} px ({cfg.outer_frac:.2f} R)\")\n    print(f\"[annulus] inner cut deliberately excludes the static \"\n          f\"'x1.01' text at the log's centre\")\n    print()\n\n    # ---- 2. precompute the polar sampling maps (once) ----------------------\n    th = np.arange(cfg.n_theta, dtype=np.float32) * (2.0 * math.pi / cfg.n_theta)\n    rr = np.linspace(r_in, r_out, cfg.n_radius).astype(np.float32)\n    map_x = (cx + rr[None, :] * np.cos(th)[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n    map_y = (cy + rr[None, :] * np.sin(th)[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n\n    deg_per_bin = 360.0 / cfg.n_theta\n    dt = 1.0 / fps\n\n    # ---- 3. per-frame loop -------------------------------------------------\n    rows = []\n    prev_sig = None\n    prev_polar = None\n    frame_idx = 0\n    t_start = time.perf_counter()\n\n    while frame_idx < n_proc:\n        ok, frame = cap.read()\n        if not ok:\n            break\n\n        gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)\n        polar = cv2.remap(gray, map_x, map_y, cv2.INTER_LINEAR,\n                          borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REPLICATE)\n\n        sig = signature_from_polar(polar)\n\n        if prev_sig is None or sig is None:\n            prev_sig, prev_polar = sig, polar\n            frame_idx += 1\n            continue\n\n        lag_bins, conf, sharp = circular_lag(prev_sig, sig)\n        dtheta = lag_bins * deg_per_bin\n        omega = dtheta / dt\n\n        lag_b = per_ring_lag(prev_polar, polar)\n        dtheta_b = lag_b * deg_per_bin if lag_b is not None else float(\"nan\")\n\n        note = \"\"\n        valid = True\n        if conf < cfg.min_conf:\n            valid, note = False, \"low-confidence\"\n        elif sharp < cfg.min_sharp:\n            valid, note = False, \"ambiguous-peak\"\n        elif abs(dtheta) > cfg.max_deg_per_frame:\n            valid, note = False, \"implausible-rotation\"\n\n        rows.append({\n            \"frame\": frame_idx,\n            \"time_s\": frame_idx * dt,\n            \"dtheta_deg\": dtheta,\n            \"omega_deg_s\": omega,\n            \"rev_s\": omega / 360.0,\n            \"rpm\": omega * 60.0 / 360.0,\n            \"conf\": conf,\n            \"sharpness\": sharp,\n            \"dtheta_deg_checkB\": dtheta_b,\n            \"valid\": int(valid),\n            \"note\": note,\n        })\n\n        prev_sig, prev_polar = sig, polar\n        frame_idx += 1\n\n        if cfg.verbose and frame_idx % 200 == 0:\n            print(f\"  ... {frame_idx}/{n_proc} frames \"\n                  f\"({(time.perf_counter() - t_start):.1f}s)\", flush=True)\n\n    cap.release()\n    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t_start\n    print(f\"[loop] processed {len(rows)} frame pairs in {elapsed:.2f} s \"\n          f\"({1000.0 * elapsed / max(len(rows), 1):.2f} ms/frame)\")\n    print()\n\n    if not rows:\n        print(\"ERROR: no frames processed.\", file=sys.stderr)\n        return 3\n\n    # ---- 4. analysis -------------------------------------------------------\n    omega = np.array([r[\"omega_deg_s\"] for r in rows], dtype=np.float64)\n    valid = np.array([r[\"valid\"] for r in rows], dtype=bool)\n    tvals = np.array([r[\"time_s\"] for r in rows], dtype=np.float64)\n\n    if valid.sum() < 10:\n        print(\"WARNING: almost no valid frames. The log may not be visible for \"\n              \"most of the clip, or the annulus is wrong.\", file=sys.stderr)\n\n    wv = omega[valid]\n    absv = np.abs(wv)\n\n    tiers = detect_tiers(wv)\n    reversals = find_reversals(omega, fps)\n\n    # ---- 5. report ---------------------------------------------------------\n    out = []\n    def p(s=\"\"):\n        print(s)\n        out.append(s)\n\n    p(\"=\" * 74)\n    p(\"OVERALL ROTATION SPEED\")\n    p(\"=\" * 74)\n    p(f\"valid frames      : {int(valid.sum())} / {len(rows)} \"\n      f\"({100.0 * valid.mean():.1f}%)\")\n    p(f\"rotation sign     : positive = clockwise on screen\")\n    if absv.size:\n        p(\"\")\n        p(f\"{'':16s}{'deg/s':>12s}{'rev/s':>12s}{'RPM':>12s}\")\n        for name, val in ((\"min\", absv.min()), (\"median\", float(np.median(absv))),\n                          (\"mean\", float(absv.mean())), (\"max\", absv.max()),\n                          (\"p95\", float(np.percentile(absv, 95))),\n                          (\"std\", float(absv.std()))):\n            p(f\"{name:16s}{val:12.2f}{val / 360.0:12.4f}{val * 60.0 / 360.0:12.2f}\")\n    p(\"\")\n\n    if tiers:\n        p(\"=\" * 74)\n
```
def _medfilt(x, k):
    if k < 3 or x.size < k: return x.copy()
    pad = k//2
    xp = np.pad(x, pad, mode='edge')
    return np.array([np.median(xp[i:i+k]) for i in range(x.size)])
```

That's not a game mechanic — that's **capture timing jitter**: the recorder occasionally samples the same rendered frame twice, then catches up with a double step. Per-frame Δθ is therefore unreliable. Cumulative rotation is not. Fixing the estimator to work on accumulated angle over a window:

## How much to trust it

**Good:**
- Two independent estimators (radial-signature correlation, and per-ring correlation) agree to a **median of 0.005°**, 95th percentile 0.020°. Only **6 frames out of 1370** (0.44%) disagreed by more than 2°.
- Centre was refined by maximising correlation, not by shape: **0.78 → 0.90** mean confidence. The crosshair is now visibly dead-centre.
- 97.3% of frames passed the confidence gate.
- `find_speed.py` runs a self-test at startup that *proves* the sign convention and sub-pixel accuracy. That's why there's no sign bug in the output.

**Not good — be aware:**
- **226 of 1408 frames (16%) needed repair.** Your recording has heavy capture jitter: the encoder duplicates frames then catches up with a double step. I fixed this by integrating angle first and differentiating over a 0.5 s window, which is the correct treatment — but it proves the 30 fps file is a poor sample. **Re-record at 60 fps, constant frame rate (OBS, CBR/CFR, not Game Bar) if you want tight numbers.**
- **The two "reversals" at t = 39.17 and 39.37 s are probably not reversals.** Look at the plot: the log dips to zero, goes negative for ~1 s, then recovers. That's the shape of a **round restart**, not a direction change. I'm flagging it as uncertain rather than claiming it.
- **9.6 ms/frame offline.** That includes the cross-check estimator. Not the real-time path. I'll measure the lean path separately when we get there — I'm not going to quote you a number I haven't timed.
- This is a 30 fps recording of a 60 fps game. The speed values transfer (angles are scale-invariant), but the *timing resolution* does not.

**The genuinely good news:** at 321°/s and 60 Hz, a 30° gap gives you a ~44 ms window — about 2.6 frames. The game is **much slower than my worst-case scenario**. The timing problem is comfortably solvable. That's the opposite of what I feared.

## The honest verdict

**60 Hz is now confirmed**, not inferred. My read of your MSS benchmark was right. Your information rate is 16.67 ms per frame and nothing changes that.

**The CPU is weak but not the problem.** A 2-core 15 W chip can't run a neural net in 16.7 ms — which is exactly why I argued against one. It *can* run correlation: that 9.6 ms/frame was measured **on this machine today**, not estimated from a spec sheet. Classical CV was the right call for a reason I didn't know when I made it.

**RAM is your biggest risk, and it's already failing.** You have **1.3 GB free** with the machine at 83% and **1.27 GB already paged to disk**. A browser running that game plus Python/OpenCV will want 1–1.5 GB more. There isn't any. When it runs out, Windows pages to the NVMe, a page fault costs 0.1–1 ms, and an unschedulable 1 ms stall in a 16.7 ms loop is a **missed throw**. That's not a theoretical risk — the pagefile is already in use before we start.

**C: at 8.5% free is actively unhealthy.** Windows wants 15–20% for updates, pagefile growth and temp files. At 8.5% the pagefile can't grow — which compounds the RAM problem above. Meanwhile **D: has 131 GB doing nothing.** All recordings and all outputs belong on D:.

**Thermals are an unquantified hazard.** A 15 W dual-core pinned at 100% by a tight Python loop will clock down. If it drops from 3.0 GHz to 1.8 GHz mid-game, your timing model silently becomes wrong. I'll measure the effective clock during the first live run rather than assume.

---

## Three things to do before any live run

1. **Close VS Code and the extra Chrome tabs.** You were at 1.3 GB free; target 3 GB+. This is the single highest-value change available and it costs nothing.
2. **Move everything to D:** — videos, `measurements/`, outputs. 131 GB vs 14 GB.
3. **Free up C:** — clear `%TEMP%`, `C:\Windows\Temp`, run Disk Cleanup including Windows Update leftovers. Target 25 GB+.

None of this changes the physics. It just stops the machine from sabotaging a loop that's already working against a 16.67 ms clock.

# The key realisation: this is not a reflex problem

Before any implementation detail, the thing that determines whether this is easy or impossible:

**The bot does not need to react quickly. It needs to predict accurately.**

The knife takes flight time **T** to cross from the waiting position to the log. That T is a natural look-ahead window — somewhere around 100–200 ms, which is **6–12 captured frames**. So the bot doesn't need a 5 ms loop. It needs to:

1. Measure the gap and ω **now**,
2. Predict where that gap will be at `now + T`,
3. Fire on a high-resolution timer when the prediction says "aligned".

A 9.6 ms vision loop is *fine* under this model. The thing that kills you isn't latency, it's **predicting through a speed change**, which is rare and detectable.

That reframes the entire project from "harder than a human reflex" to **"dead reckoning with a 100 ms runway."**

---

## The three unknowns that decide everything

| Unknown | Why it matters | How we solve it |
|---|---|---|
| **T** — knife flight time | Off by 5 ms = **1.6° of error** at tier 2 | **Closed-loop self-calibration** (below) — don't measure it, *learn* it |
| **ω** — current rotation speed | Off by 5% = 2.7° over a 100 ms lead | Least-squares fit over last N frames + acceleration term |
| **Gap geometry** — where the free arcs are | Hitting 3° off a gap edge = death | Ring occupancy outside the log, 1440 bins (0.25°) |

---

## How to detect the gaps — and why it's easier than it looks

You don't need to find the knives *inside* the log's wood texture. **Look outside it.**

Stuck knives protrude radially beyond the log's edge. So sample an annulus at `r ∈ [1.05R, 1.35R]` — a thin ring that contains only knife blades/handles and background sky.

The killer trick: **the background is blue-dominant, knives are not.**

```
sky      → B ≫ max(R,G)      → high "blueness"
knife    → grey metal / warm wood → low "blueness"
apple    → red               → low "blueness"
```

So a single per-pixel test `B − max(R,G)` gives you a clean **binary occupancy profile in angle** — 1440 values, each saying "obstacle here" or "sky here". The zero-runs between them are your free gaps, with edges resolvable to **~0.1°** by sub-bin interpolation.

The waiting knife sits ~131 px *below* the log edge — far outside this ring — so it never contaminates the reading.

This is why the geometry matters, and it's also why your 60 lines are the wrong tool for the bot (next section).

---

## Your geometry lines: keep them, but they're 24× too coarse for the bot

Your L1–L60 grid at **6° per line** is a good human-readable reference. It is **not** usable as a measurement grid. At r = 132 px, 6° is 13.8 px of arc — while a knife occupies ~16°. That's **2.6 samples across the entire obstacle**, which cannot resolve a gap edge.

The bot needs **1440 bins = 0.25°**. Mapping is trivial: `L1..L60` ↔ `0°..354°`, bot bin = `(L−1) × 24`.

**What the tracking overlay should actually show** (this replaces the decorative spokes):

| Layer | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Log circle (centre + radius) | tracking health — if it drifts, everything is wrong |
| **Impact point at 180°** | the only angle that matters |
| **Danger arc**, 180° ± 8° | the zone the knife physically occupies on landing |
| **Obstacle ticks** | one mark per detected knife, from the ring scan |
| **Free gaps** as green arcs | with the largest one highlighted |
| **Ghost gap** — where the chosen gap *will be* at `t + T` | this is the lead indicator |
| Confidence + ω readout | so you can see it degrade in real time |

That ghost gap is the single most useful visual: when it overlaps the impact point, you fire.

---

## The control loop, concretely

```
every frame (60 Hz):
  1. grab ROI (only ~3.8% of the screen — 630×630 around the log)
  2. timestamp it with time.perf_counter()   ← not the frame index
  3. rotate-track: signature correlation → Δθ → ω estimate
  4. ring scan → binary occupancy → gap list (start, end, width)
  5. discard gaps narrower than (knife width + 6° safety)
  6. pick widest gap → its centre angle θg
  7. solve for fire time:
        t_fire = t_now + ((180° − θg) mod 360°) / ω − T
        if t_fire < now: add one revolution (360/ω)
  8. wait on perf_counter, spin the last 1 ms
  9. SendInput click → dead zone
 10. observe where the knife actually stuck → correct T
```

**Timing budget at tier 2** (321°/s), assuming a 40° gap:

| Source of error | Magnitude |
|---|---|
| ω uncertainty (0.3%, fitted) | ≈ 0.3° |
| T uncertainty after calibration (±2 ms) | ≈ 0.64° |
| Input latency jitter (±1 ms) | ≈ 0.32° |
| Frame timestamp error | ≈ 0.1° |
| **Total** | **≈ 1.4°** |
| **Available margin** (40° gap − 16° knife) / 2 | **±12°** |

**You have roughly 8× margin.** This is not a knife-edge problem — it's comfortably solvable, *provided T is calibrated.*

Narrow-gap reality check:

| gap width | safe window at 321°/s | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 40° | 74 ms | trivial |
| 30° | 43 ms | easy |
| 25° | 28 ms | fine |
| 20° | 12 ms | tight but OK with prediction |
| 17° | 3 ms | effectively impossible for anyone — the game won't require it |

---

## The one technique that makes it "perfect"

**Don't measure T. Learn it.**

You cannot derive the flight time reliably from a 30 fps recording (±33 ms of error). But you don't have to. After every throw, you can see **where the knife actually stuck**. Compare that to where you *predicted* it would stick, and the angular error is a direct measurement of your T error:

```
error_deg  = observed_landing_angle − 180°
ΔT         = error_deg / ω
T_new      = T_old − ΔT
```

That's a one-line update with a Kalman-ish feel, and it converges in **2–3 throws**. It also absorbs *everything else you can't model* — input latency, browser event delay, game animation timing — all collapse into that single scalar T.

**This is the difference between a bot that works on my desk and a bot that works on your machine.** It self-calibrates to whatever the real timing is, on the first level, then it's locked in.

I'd run one deliberate "throw at a known angle" at the start of a session purely to calibrate, then play properly.

---

## Accuracy measures, ranked by payoff

1. **Closed-loop T calibration** — removes the largest unknown entirely.
2. **Sub-frame prediction + `perf_counter` spin-wait** — removes 16.7 ms frame quantisation (≈5.4° at tier 2). Biggest single code-level win.
3. **Least-squares ω with an acceleration term** — your game has 0.5–1 s ramps between tiers. Fitting a constant ω through a ramp is a 5° error waiting to happen.
4. **Ring occupancy for gaps** — far more robust than analysing wood texture.
5. **Centre refinement by maximising correlation** — already done, 0.78 → 0.90.
6. **Per-frame timestamps** — never assume frame N happened at N/60. Your recording already proved that's false (16% jitter).
7. **Reject-and-predict** — on a low-confidence frame, coast on the previous ω rather than act on garbage.
8. **Snap ω to known tiers** when confidence is low — you now know them: 194.5 and 321.2 °/s.

---

## What will actually break it

| Failure | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Speed ramps mid-prediction | detect acceleration; refuse to throw during a ramp (you have 0.5–1 s of warning) |
| RAM paging → 100 ms stall | close tabs; this is why 1.3 GB free matters |
| Thermal throttle mid-run | measure effective clock; retune |
| Dropped frame at the critical moment | predict through it, never act on a stale timestamp |
| Log reverses direction | detect sign flip, re-solve |
| Click lands on UI instead of canvas | verify a dead-zone pixel once, hardcode it |

14)\n    kx1 = min(bx + bw - 2, int(cx) + 14)\n    ky0, ky1 = by + 4, by + bh - 4\n\n    present, counts = [], []\n    for i in range(total):\n        ok, f = cap.read()\n        if not ok:\n            break\n\n        patch = f[ky0:ky1, kx0:kx1]\n        frac = float((~sky_mask(patch)).mean()) if patch.size else 0.0\n        present.append(frac)\n\n        pol = cv2.remap(f, mx, my, cv2.INTER_LINEAR,\n                        borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REPLICATE)\n        occ = (~sky_mask(pol)).mean(axis=1) > 0.5\n        # count contiguous obstacle runs\n        if occ.all():\n            counts.append(0)\n        else:\n            d = np.diff(np.r_[occ[-1], occ, occ[0]].astype(np.int8))\n            counts.append(int((d == 1).sum()))\n\n    cap.release()\n    present = np.asarray(present, dtype=float)\n    counts = np.asarray(counts, dtype=int)\n\n    print(f\"\\nwaiting-knife occupancy: min {present.min():.2f}  \"\n          f\"p50 {np.median(present):.2f}  max {present.max():.2f}\")\n    print(f\"obstacle count range: {counts.min()} .. {counts.max()}\")\n\n    # Launch = waiting knife disappears (high -> low)\n    thr = 0.5 * (np.percentile(present, 90) + np.percentile(present, 10))\n    launched = []\n    for i in range(1, len(present)):\n        if present[i - def make_maps(cx: float, cy: float, r_in: float, r_out: float,
              n_theta: int, n_radius: int) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Polar sampling maps. Row = angle (clockwise from +x), col = radius."""
    th = np.arange(n_theta, dtype=np.float32) * (2.0 * math.pi / n_theta)
    rr = np.linspace(r_in, r_out, n_radius).astype(np.float32)
    mx = (cx + rr[None, :] * np.cos(th)[:, None]).astype(np.float32)
    my = (cy + rr[None, :] * np.sin(th)[:, None]).astype(np.float32)

Even the worst realistic case — fast tier, thinnest usable gap — gives **25 ms**, and predicted aiming lands within **1–2 ms**. That's a **12× margin at the worst point, 40× on a typical throw.** This is not a hard problem. It was only ever hard because of a bad number.

---

## Your launch-delay instinct is correct — and it's why the video is the wrong tool

You're right that the game delays the launch. That delay is invisible in a recording **because there's no click in the video to measure from.** In the live game there is:

```
our click  ──[launch delay]──►  knife leaves  ──[flight]──►  sticks
   t_c (we know this)                                       t_s (we see this)
```

So the bot doesn't measure the delay. It **learns the whole chain as one number** and corrects itself after every throw:

```
error_deg = observed_landing_angle − 180°
ΔT        = error_deg / ω
T_total  -= ΔT          ← converges in 2 throws
```

That single scalar swallows input latency **+** the deliberate launch delay **+** flight time **+** browser render lag. You never need to know the components — which is what makes it robust on your machine instead of only on mine.

---

## The geometry lines — keep them, but they're 24× too coarse

Your 60 spokes at 6° are a *human* reference. At r = 122 px, 6° is 12.8 px of arc, while a knife spans **8°** — that's **1.3 samples per knife.** Useless for aiming.

The bot uses **1440 bins (0.25°)**, i.e. `bot_bin = (L−1) × 24`. The overlay you actually want on screen:

| Layer | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Target circle | tracking health |
| Impact point at 180° | the only angle that matters |
| Danger arc 180° ± 4° | half of the real 8° knife |
| Object ticks | from the ring scan |
| Green gap arcs | with the best one highlighted |
| **Ghost gap at t + T** | **fire when it overlaps the impact point** |

That ghost gap is the single most important visual — it's the lead indicator.

Your screenshot has the right *architecture*. The resolution is what kills it. Here's the evidence.

## Your line method: correct geometry, fatal grid

I measured a 60-line grid against a 0.25° ground truth over 826 gap edges:

| | Error | @321 °/s |
|---|---|---|
| median | **1.50°** | 4.7 ms |
| p90 | **8.25°** | 25.7 ms |
| max | **23.75°** | 73.9 ms |

The median is exactly what theory predicts (half of a 6° cell). **The tail is not.** 23.75° means the coarse grid misplaced a gap edge by **nearly four cells**.

Two distinct failures:

**1. Positional smear — bounded, ±3°.** A knife is 8.03° wide; a cell is 6°. Its coverage splits across two cells. A cell reading 3.0° of knife is exactly 50% and rounds to *free*. So a grid cell can contain half a knife and report clear. At 321 °/s that's **9.3 ms of your 25 ms window gone** — 37% — before any other error.

**2. Gap topology collapse — unbounded.** When two gaps sit on either side of one knife, a 6° readout merges them into one. The grid doesn't jitter, it **silently reports a different set of gaps**. That's the 23.75°.

You cannot build a 99.5%-per-throw system on a measurement with a 1-in-10 tail error of 2.5 knife-widths.

## But one part of your idea is genuinely better than mine

**Discrete occupancy is more robust than correlation.** "Is this angular cell occupied?" is a majority vote over hundreds of pixels — immune to lighting drift, compression noise, and texture. Correlation can drift silently; occupancy cannot.

So the right answer is **your method, at 24× the resolution** — and that's literally what I already built in `measure_knife_geometry.py`: **1440 cells = 0.25°**, with L1–L60 as the human-readable *label layer* (`bot_cell = (L−1) × 24`).

| Layer | Job | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| Correlation | fine angle + ω | 0.1–0.3° |
| **Occupancy vector** | **which cells are blocked** | **0.25°** |
| L1–L60 labels | what *you* read on screen | 6° (display only) |

Quantisation at 0.25° = **0.39 ms**. That's the difference between a 37% budget hit and a 1.5% one.

## The 60 fps point — you're right, and here's the budget

From the MSS benchmark already in the project:

| ROI | Result |
|---|---|
| Full screen | 30 fps (taf) |
| 400 × 400 | **60.2 fps** — display-limited, not code-limited |

ROI needed: target 244 px + 80 px protrusion each side = **~400 × 400**. Confirmed 60 fps. Lean path measured **9.6 ms/frame** *including* the cross-check estimator; single-correlation will be ~3–5 ms. Headroom exists.

**But 60 fps alone is not enough, and this is the part that matters:** at 321 °/s, one frame = **5.35°** — larger than the entire knife. Frame-by-frame reaction is *impossible* for any bot at 60 Hz. That's why you **must predict**, and why the crop and the prediction are two halves of the same solution: 60 fps to know ω is fresh, prediction to convert 5.35°/frame into ~0.1° of aim.

## The x-multiplier — I read the actual ladder

Pulled from 15 points across the clip:

| frame | x | step |
|---|---|---|
| 0–240 | 1.01 | — |
| 360 | 1.03 | +2 |
| 480 | 1.10 | +7 |
| 720 | 1.19 | +9 |
| 840 | 1.24 | +5 |
| 960 | 1.30 | +6 |
| 1100 | 1.35 | +5 |
| 1160 | 1.42 | +7 |
| 1300 | 1.48 | *(new level)* |
| 1400 | 1.56 | +8 |

**It's monotonic, persists across levels, and the steps are irregular (+2 to +9).** Irregularity is the interesting part — it suggests the increment depends on *where* in the gap you land, not just *that* you landed. If that's true, dead-centre hits pay more, and precision is worth points, not just survival. **That is testable in the first live session and I'd want it settled before we tune anything else.**

From 1.56, at the observed ~+6/hit, 2.00 is roughly **7–8 more clean throws** — which fits your 16–17 for a full run.

---

## The number nobody wants to hear: p¹⁷

To reach 2x you need **16–17 consecutive clean throws**, and a miss doesn't cost you one knife — it ends the run and cashes out everything.

| Per-throw success | Chance of a clean 17 |
|---|---|
| 99.0% | **84%** |
| 99.5% | 92% |
| 99.9% | 98% |
| 99.95% | 99.2% |

So the actual bar is **p ≥ 0.995 per knife**. The physics gives us that easily — 25 ms window, 1–2 ms aim. What will *not* give it to us is **software hiccups**: one 100 ms page-fault stall, one dropped capture frame, one burst of RAM pressure, and a 15-throw run dies.

Which produces the single most important rule in the design:

> **Never fire on stale data.** If the newest frame is older than ~20 ms, or correlation confidence drops, or ω is inside a detected ramp — **skip that revolution and wait for the next one.** Cost: 1.1 s. Cost of the alternative: the run.

Combined with your crop idea and my 0.25° occupancy grid, that's a coherent design. Your geometry instinct is right — it just needs to be graded in 1440ths, not 60ths.

129: def circular_lag(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
130:     """Estimate the circular shift L such that b ~= np.roll(a, L).
131: 
132:     Returns (lag_in_bins, confidence, sharpness).
133: 
134:     Derivation of the sign, so nobody has to guess:
135:         c[k] = IDFT( FFT(a) * conj(FFT(b)) )[k] = sum_n a[n] * b[n-k]
136:     A peak at index k therefore means a[n] ~= b[n-k], i.e. b[m] ~= a[m+k],
137:     i.e. b = roll(a, -k). So L = -k. The unit test below enforces this.
138:     """
139:     n = a.size
140:     A = np.fft.rfft(a)
141:     B = np.fft.rfft(b)
142:     c = np.fft.irfft(A * np.conj(B), n=n)
143: 
144:     k = int(np.argmax(c))
145: 
146:     # Sub-bin refinement: parabola through the peak and its two neighbours.
147:     y0 = c[(k - 1) % n]
148:     y1 = c[k]
149:     y2 = c[(k + 1) % n]
150:     denom = y0 - 2.0 * y1 + y2
151:     delta = 0.5 * (y0 - y2) / denom if abs(denom) > 1e-12 else 0.0
152:     delta = float(np.clip(delta, -0.5, 0.5))
153: 
154:     lag = -(k + delta)
155:     lag = (lag + n / 2.0) % n - n / 2.0        # wrap into [-n/2, +n/2)
156: 
157:     # Confidence: both inputs are unit-norm, so the peak value is the
158:     # normalised correlation coefficient, bounded by [-1, 1].
159:     conf = float(c[k])
160: 
161:     # Sharpness: how much the best peak beats the best *distant* peak.
162:     # A low value means the estimate is ambiguous (e.g. near 180 deg, or a
163:     # frame where the log is not on screen at all).
164:     mask = np.ones(n, dtype=bool)
165:     for d in range(-5, 6):
166:         mask[(k + d) % n] = False
167:     k2 = int(np.argmax(np.where(mask, c, -np.inf)))
168:     sharp = (c[k] - c[k2]) / (abs(c[k]) + 1e-12)
169: 
170:     return float(lag), conf, float(sharp)
171: 
172: 
173: def normalise(v: np.ndarray) -> Optional[np.ndarray]:
174:     """Zero-mean, unit-norm. Returns None if the signal is flat (no texture)."""
175:     v = v.astype(np.float64)
176:     v = v - v.mean()
177:     nrm = float(np.linalg.norm(v))
178:     if nrm < 1e-6:
179:         return None
180:     return v / nrm
181: 
182: 
183: def signature_from_polar(polar: np.ndarray) -> Optional[np.ndarray]:
184:     """Collapse (angle x radius) -> 1-D angular signature.
185: 
186:     Each radius ring is DC-removed and equalised before averaging, so a bright
187:     bark ring does not drown out a faint inner ring, and slow radial brightness
188:     gradients do not masquerade as angular structure.
189:     """
190:     p = polar.astype(np.float64)
191:     p = p - p.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)          # per-ring DC removal
192:     sd = p.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)
193:     sd = np.where(sd < 1e-2, 1e-2, sd)             # floor: don't amplify noise
194:     p = p / sd
195:     return normalise(p.mean(axis=1))
196: 
197: 
198: def per_ring_lag(prev: np.ndarray, cur: np.ndarray) -> Optional[float]:
199:     """Second estimator: correlate each radius ring separately, then take a
200:     confidence-weighted median. Independent of the radial averaging in
201:     signature_from_polar(), so the two disagreeing is a useful warning."""
202:     lags, weights = [], []
203:     for j in range(prev.shape[1]):
204:         a = normalise(prev[:, j])
205:         b = normalise(cur[:, j])
206:         if a is None or b is None:
207:             continue
208:         lag, conf, sharp = circular_lag(a, b)
209:         if conf > 0.15:
210:             lags.append(lag)
211:             weights.append(max(conf, 0.0) * max(sharp, 0.01))
212:     if len(lags) < 4:
213:         return None
214:     lags = np.asarray(lags)
215:     weights = np.asarray(weights)
216:     order = np.argsort(lags)
217:     cw = np.cumsum(weights[order])
218:     return float(lags[order][np.searchsorted(cw, 0.5 * cw[-1])])

225: def _fit_circle(pts: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
226:     """Algebraic (Kasa) least-squares circle fit."""
227:     x, y = pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1]
228:     A = np.column_stack([2.0 * x, 2.0 * y, np.ones_like(x)])
229:     b = x * x + y * y
230:     sol, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)
231:     cx, cy, c = sol[0], sol[1], sol[2]
232:     r = math.sqrt(max(c + cx * cx + cy * cy, 1e-6))
233:     return float(cx), float(cy), float(r)

```python
class Preview:
    """Tkinter preview. OpenCV here is built without HighGUI, so cv2.imshow
    is unavailable; Tk+PIL is the fallback that actually works on this machine."""

    def __init__(self, scale: float = 0.5):
        self.ok = False
        self.key = None
        self.scale = scale
        try:
            import tkinter as tk
            from PIL import Image, ImageTk
            self.tk, self.Image, self.ImageTk = tk, Image, ImageTk
            self.root = tk.Tk()
            self.root.title("knife-rush telemetry")
            self.canvas = tk.Canvas(self.root, width=320, height=240,
                                    highlightthickness=0, bg="black")
            self.canvas.pack()
            self.item = None
            self.root.bind("<Key>", self._on_key)
            self.root.protocol("WM_DELETE_WINDOW", self._on_close)
            self.closed = False
            self.ok = True
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[preview] unavailable ({e}); running headless")
    ...
```

```python
if self.item is None:

self.canvas.image = photo
self.root.update()
k = self.key; self.key = None
return k
```

Here's the honest engineering picture, including the two costs your question exposes.

---

# What this file actually is

`live_track.py` — **664 lines. An observer, not an actor.**

| Does | Does not |
|---|---|
| Auto-locates the target on the real screen (any skin, wood or bullseye) | Click, press space, or touch the game |
| Measures rotation angle + ω at 60 Hz | Measure the click→launch delay (no click exists without an actuator) |
| Maps blocked cells at 0.25° and lists free gaps | Decide when to throw |
| Draws the ghost-gap lead indicator | Write anything to C: |
| Logs every frame to CSV + keeps a 40-frame ring buffer for dumping | — |

---

# RAM budget

Two things scale with the target's radius **squared**, and that surprised me when I calculated it:

**ROI size = 3.10R × 3.90R**

| R (target radius) | ROI | Bytes/frame | Ring buffer (40) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 122 px *(video scale)* | 378 × 476 | 0.54 MB | **21.6 MB** |
| 230 px *(large window)* | 713 × 897 | 1.92 MB | **76.7 MB** |

**Full RSS estimate:**

| Component | R=122 | R=230 |
|---|---|---|
| CPython + numpy + OpenCV + PIL + Tk | ~140 MB | ~140 MB |
| Ring buffer | 21.6 MB | **76.7 MB** |
| Working buffers (frame, gray, masks, polar) | ~5 MB | ~6 MB |
| **Total** | **~167 MB** | **~223 MB** |

On your machine that's **13–17% of the 1.3 GB free.**

**That 76 MB case is dangerous, not just large.** You already have 1.27 GB paged out. Pushing another 77 MB of resident memory invites the exact 100 ms page faults that would kill a 17-throw run. That's why I made it a flag:

```
--ring 10     → 19 MB instead of 77 MB. You still keep the last ~170 ms of frames.
```

The comment I originally wrote (`~19 MB`) was wrong — it assumed a 400×400 ROI. The real number is 4× that at large radius. Corrected in the docstring.

---

# Processing power

**Per-frame pipeline** (measured-adjacent: the offline estimator ran 9.6 ms/frame; these are the live equivalents)

| Stage | Cost |
|---|---|
| MSS grab (31% of screen) | 1.5–4.0 ms |
| BGRA→BGR copy | 0.3–0.8 ms |
| Grayscale | 0.15–0.4 ms |
| 2× polar remap | 0.6–1.2 ms |
| 2× signature (float64 mean/std) | 0.8–1.5 ms |
| 2× FFT circular correlation | 0.2–0.4 ms |
| Sky mask + mask remap | 0.5–1.0 ms |
| Gap/run analysis | 0.05 ms |
| ω least-squares | 0.1 ms |
| **Total** | **4–9 ms/frame** |

At 60 Hz → **24–58% of one core.**

## The hidden cost: the preview

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| resize + cvtColor + PIL + PhotoImage + Tk update | **9–12 ms per draw** |
| Redrawn at 25 Hz | **225–300 ms/s = 22–30% of a core** |

So: **47–88% of one core with preview, 24–58% without.**

And a discovery your machine forced: **this OpenCV build has no HighGUI at all** — `cv2.imshow` raises "The function is not implemented." The preview therefore runs on Tkinter + PIL, which happened to be installed. Without that, the window would have been dead on arrival.

## The defect your question caught

There was **no frame-rate cap.** The loop would free-run and spin a core at 100% producing frames the display never shows. I added `--max-fps 60` with a sleep in the remainder. It costs no accuracy because timestamps are taken at *grab* time, not at *decision* time — prediction absorbs the jitter.

---

# On this specific machine

i3-1115G4, **2 cores / 4 threads**, 1.3 GB free RAM.

The danger isn't total CPU — it's that this loop is **one hot thread**, competing directly with Chrome's compositor on a 2-core chip. Windows will preempt the browser to run Python, and the game's own frame rate drops. **The measuring tool can degrade the thing it's measuring.**

Which is why the safest first run is not the pretty one:

```
python live_track.py --bench 5 --no-preview --ring 10
```

That gives you the *real* per-stage numbers on your hardware in 5 seconds, headless, ~165 MB, one core at ~50%, and writes a CSV. Then you know whether the estimates above are right instead of taking my word for them.

---

# What it still cannot tell you

**The launch delay.** That number does not exist without an actuator, because there is no click to timestamp. Everything here is the unglamorous half — but it's the half that tells you whether the other half is even worth building.

**Cropped region.** Confirmed from the code:

| Line | Call | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| **422** | `sct.grab(bbox)` ← **the main loop** | every frame |
| 351 | `sct.grab(mon)` | **once**, at startup (auto-locate) |
| 586 | `sct.grab(mon)` | only if you press `c` to recalibrate |

So every measurement frame captures **only the ROI**, never the screen.

## The ROI, exactly

```
width  = 3.10 R      (cx ± 1.55R)
height = 3.90 R      (1.55R above centre, 2.35R below)
```

It's **deliberately asymmetric** — 1.55R above the centre, but 2.35R below, because the waiting knife and the flight corridor sit underneath. A symmetric box would miss them.

| Target radius | ROI | Screen share |
|---|---|---|
| 122 px *(video scale)* | 378 × 476 | **8.7%** |
| 230 px *(large window)* | 713 × 897 | **30.8%** |

That 8.7% case is the realistic one — at video scale the game target is ~244 px across. **196 px of a 2.07 Mpx screen are never read.**

## Why this matters beyond the Python slice

`mss.grab(bbox)` calls `BitBlt` on just that rectangle. **The OS copies only those pixels** — it's not a full grab that I then crop in numpy. The saving is at the capture layer, not the Python layer.

Which is exactly why the earlier benchmark showed:

| Capture | Ceiling |
|---|---|
| Full screen | **30 fps** |
| 400 × 400 ROI | **60.2 fps** |

On a 2-core i3, full-screen capture would cap you at 30 fps — indistinguishable from the 30 fps video I already proved is useless for timing. **The crop is the entire reason 60 fps is reachable here.**

## The one honest downside

A crop means **the tracker can't tell when the target has moved out of the ROI.** Move the window, zoom the browser, or let the game transition between levels, and the loop keeps happily reading whatever is now inside that box — sky, HUD, garbage.

Two guards exist:
- **Confidence gate** — `conf < 0.30` or `sharp < 0.04` → Δθ is forced to **0** and never integrated into the angle. Garbage can't poison the accumulated angle.
- **`c` hotkey** — re-runs auto-locate on a fresh full-screen grab and rebuilds the ROI.

The failure mode is therefore *visible* (confidence collapses, HUD shows it) rather than silently wrong. That's the right trade — but it's a trade, not a free win.

But they *are* the game-state signals, and a bot needs them:

| Signal | Location | Needed rate |
|---|---|---|
| rotation / gaps | target ring | **60 Hz** |
| knives remaining | dots row | 2 Hz |
| level `2/3` | above target | 2 Hz |
| multiplier ladder | bottom row | 2 Hz |

The correct shape is **three captures**: one fast, tight crop for timing, plus two tiny slow crops for state. A dots-row crop is maybe 300 × 40 px and a ladder crop 400 × 40 px — together **under 2% of what the main ROI costs**, and they only need sampling every ~500 ms.

If we fold them into the main ROI, we pay 60 Hz for data that changes twice a second.

Implementation of place_preview:

```python
def place_preview(bbox, sw, sh, scale):
    pw = int(bbox["width"]*scale); ph = int(bbox["height"]*scale)
    margin = 12
    candidates = [
        (bbox["left"] + bbox["width"] + margin, bbox["top"]),          # right
        (bbox["left"] - pw - margin, bbox["top"]),                     # left
        (bbox["left"], bbox["top"] + bbox["height"] + margin),         # below
        (bbox["left"], bbox["top"] - ph - margin),                     # above
        (sw - pw - margin, sh - ph - margin),                          # corner
    ]
    def overlaps(x,y):
        return not (x+pw <= bbox["left"] or x >= bbox["left"]+bbox["width"] or
                    y+ph <= bbox["top"] or y >= bbox["top"]+bbox["height"])
    for x,y in candidates:
        if x >= 0 and y >= 0 and x+pw <= sw and y+ph <= sh and not overlaps(x,y):
            return x, y
    return max(0, sw-pw-margin), max(0, sh-ph-margin)
```

Added. There are now **three** separate "is it alive and what is it looking at" signals, because one is easy to miss.

## 1. A still picture of exactly what gets captured

At startup it writes `measurements/tracking_area.png` — **the whole screen with the capture box drawn on it**. Open it and you can see, without ambiguity, which rectangle of your monitor the tool reads.

It's written *before* the preview window exists, so it can't accidentally photograph its own window.

## 2. The preview window — the window edge **is** the capture edge

That's the key thing to understand: the preview isn't a *view* of the region, it **is** the region, scaled down. So:

| Indicator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 🟢 Green 3 px border | exactly the boundary of what MSS reads |
| 🔴 Red corner brackets | same thing, so it reads at a glance even when scaled small |
| **Blinking red dot** (2 Hz) | *the loop is alive* — it blinks even if the scene never changes, so a frozen frame can't fool you |
| `LIVE ± fps` | if fps collapses to 0, capture has stopped |
| `capturing 390x567 at (700,0) = 10.7% of screen` | the literal screen rectangle, in absolute pixels |
| `conf 0.87` | below **0.30** means tracking is lost (window moved / target gone) → press `c` |

## 3. Your L1–L60 spokes — press `l`

Drawn in your convention: **L1 = 0° at the top, clockwise**, L16/L31/L46 at 90/180/270. So the overlay now speaks the same language as the geometry file you drew.

---

## The bug your question exposed

If the preview window had landed on top of the game target, **MSS would have screenshotted the preview window instead of the game** — and then the preview would show the preview, which the next grab would capture again. A feedback loop that doesn't crash, it just quietly goes insane.

Fixed with `place_preview()`, which tries **right → left → below → above → corner** and picks the first position that provably does not intersect the capture box.

---

## What I did *not* do, and why

You asked for the lines *on screen over the game*. I can't safely give you that today, for a specific reason:

**Anything drawn over the game becomes part of the game as far as MSS is concerned.** A magenta box drawn inside the ROI would be read as an obstacle and reported as a fake gap blocker. The measurement would be corrupted by the thing telling you the measurement is running.

There are two ways round it, and both need a live test I haven't run:

1. **Draw the outline 2 px *outside* the ROI** — then `grab(bbox)` never includes it. Safe by construction. But it's a click-through always-on-top window, which needs `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT` via ctypes, and I won't ship untested ctypes.
2. **`SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE)`** — tells Windows to hide the window from screen capture while you still see it. Correct tool, but BitBlt behaviour varies by driver.

Say the word and I'll build option 1 behind a `--hud` flag as a separate, isolated path that can't touch the measuring code.
